subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Swedish Coffee Experiment
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Swedish Coffee Experiment usable.

hook.text: In the 1750s, Sweden's King Gustav III tried to prove coffee was poison—using an experiment on condemned prisoners.

buildup.text: Two identical twins were sentenced to death. One was ordered to drink three pots of coffee daily, the other three pots of tea.

discovery.text: The experiment was monitored by physicians for years. Both prisoners survived long beyond expectations—outliving their doctors.

twist.text: The tea drinker died first—at age 83. The coffee drinker lived even longer. Coffee was vindicated, and the ban was dropped.

climax.text: King Gustav III was assassinated in 1792—long before the experiment concluded. He never saw coffee's acquittal.

punchline.text: The king died. The doctors died. The coffee drinker lived longest. Case closed.

quiz.question: What happened in the Swedish coffee experiment with twin prisoners?
options: Both lived past 80—the tea drinker died first, vindicating coffee

details.summary: King Gustav III of Sweden conducted an experiment to prove coffee was poisonous by sentencing twins to death, commuting one to drink only coffee and the other only tea for life. Both outlived the doctors monitoring them, and Gustav himself was assassinated before the experiment ended.
details.whyItMatters: This bizarre royal experiment is coffee history's most famous failed attempt to prove caffeine's danger, and Sweden ironically became one of the world's top coffee-consuming nations.
takeaways: Gustav III sentenced twins to lifelong coffee and tea consumption
Both prisoners outlived the monitoring physicians
Sweden is now one of the world's highest per capita coffee consumers

faq.question: What was King Gustav III trying to prove with the coffee experiment?
faq.answer: Gustav believed coffee was harmful to health and wanted scientific evidence to support a ban. By comparing a lifelong coffee drinker to a tea drinker, he hoped to demonstrate that coffee shortened life, but the results contradicted his hypothesis.

faq.question: How did Sweden eventually become one of the biggest coffee-consuming nations?
faq.answer: Despite multiple attempted bans throughout the 18th and 19th centuries, Swedes stubbornly continued drinking coffee. The cultural tradition of fika, a daily coffee break with pastries, eventually became a beloved national institution.
